p: On the Sunday morning after, Kit opened the log Vern had handed her unasked in the heritage room. It was from March 2001. His Doppler had quit, and he'd worked a crosswind by hand: a right triangle of five hundred, a hundred forty and four eighty. The last line said he'd pointed the jet sixteen degrees left to go straight. He'd pointed into the thing pushing him, and Kit had spent seven years pointing away from hers.

At his kitchen table Vern handed her four sets of math problems. She ran each one on the egg timer at the real test's twenty two minutes, then went back over her misses slowly. He showed her how he'd factored at the nav table, with the pairs written down the margin of the log.
At the water plant she read the backup generator's tank chart, worked out what the full tank held, and ordered diesel.

On a Saturday in the heritage room, Corbin Haas brought back an old altimeter he'd fixed for the display case. He told her the first week of pilot training is all from the inside of the airplane, and she knows the jet from the outside. Then he told her his mother had heard about his washout from a lady at church, the day after he'd told her it was going fine, and he asked who would hear it from Kit first. She said Graham first, and then him, if he'd pick up. He wrote his number on her math sheet. Vern had taken most of an hour to find the key to the case, and when he came back she thanked him for the hour and left it there.
Fisk texted for help before his torque retraining at the April drill. She met him at the Riverside and only asked questions, and he worked through the card himself.

The night before the practice test, Graham said he'd call time at the end of every block and say nothing else. Kit went out to the garage for a drill battery. Under the blue tarp behind the mower was a maple crib with an estate sale tag from April 2025, two springs ago, the spring he'd asked her whether this could be the year and she'd said after. She put the tarp back the way it had been. Her own story was coming first, tomorrow night, before she'd ask Graham for his. She stood in the garage until the motion light went off.
Rhonda Shaw. Kit's mother, back from chapter three. She runs a school cafeteria across the river, and she's the only one who calls Kit Kitty.
Saturday, April 3, ten to eight in the morning. Graham had been up since six. Kit could tell by the table.

He'd cleared it down to the wood. Eleven packets sat in a stack at his end, one for each block, a binder clip on every corner and the subtest written across the top in his black marker. He'd put the test together himself over three weeks of nights, out of library books and every practice page he could find, in the order the Pearson page listed and with the minutes it listed. Beside the stack was a coffee mug of sharpened pencils from his classroom, a pad of scratch paper, and the digital timer from his lab with the magnet on the back.
Her coat was on the hook by the door, the sheet still folded in the inside pocket where it had ridden for four weeks.

Graham sat down across from her and slid the first packet over. VERBAL ANALOGIES. He set the timer to eight minutes and pressed the button, and he didn't say go. He'd said what he was going to say on Friday night.
I learned my physics from an airplane, Sergeant, one bad night at a time. That's a slow way to learn it. Here's the short way.

Physical Science comes eighth, after the inventory and the break. The current Pearson page gives it 20 questions in 10 minutes. Thirty seconds apiece, and the 2015 pamphlet shows five choices on each one. It's high school science. Physics mostly, some chemistry, some earth and sky. Most of it's one step, so you know it or you don't, and if you don't, guess and go. Thirty seconds won't teach you a thing you didn't walk in with. A few want one line of arithmetic, a force or a current or a distance. Do those on scratch paper and look at your units on the way out the door.

In the 2015 practice pamphlet, Physical Science feeds no composite at all. One newer citation puts it in the CSO composite. Either way, the Pilot composite doesn't lean on it, so it isn't where your Pilot number gets made. It's still twenty questions and ten minutes of your morning, though, and some of it turns up again in Aviation Information, which does count for Pilot. I'll give it to you the way it came to me. Mostly in airplanes, mostly at night.
How the exam asks it. Thirty seconds a question. Don't know it by the time you've read the choices? Guess, and keep the clock for the ones with numbers in them.

I flew in feet and knots and pounds, and this test is in everybody else's units. Science runs on the SI, the International System of Units. Seven base units. Five you'll want cold: the meter for length, the kilogram for mass, the second for time, the kelvin for temperature, the ampere for electric current. The other two are the mole, an amount of a substance, and the candela, which is brightness. Know their names when they walk in.

Everything else gets built out of those. A newton is the force that speeds one kilogram up by a meter a second, every second. A joule's a newton pushed through a meter, so that's work, or energy. A watt's a joule every second. Power. A pascal's a newton on a square meter. Pressure. Volts and ohms and hertz come later. The miss I see most is people mixing up the jobs. A watt isn't energy, it's energy per second. A kilogram isn't a weight. It's how much stuff there is.

The prefixes ride on every unit the same. Kilo, a thousand, so a kilometer's 1,000 meters. Mega, a million. Giga, a billion. Going down, centi's a hundredth, milli a thousandth, micro a millionth, nano a billionth. A milliliter is a cubic centimeter, and a liter of water has a mass of a kilogram, and that's the handiest pair of facts in the whole system. A gallon runs about 3.8 liters, if they mix the two on you.

Try one. How many milligrams in 2.4 grams? A milligram's a thousandth of a gram, so a gram's got a thousand of them. 2,400. Got 0.0024? Then you divided, and you ought to ask yourself whether a smaller unit should give you a smaller count. It shouldn't. Little units, big count.
How the exam asks it. Smaller unit, bigger number. Say it once before you convert anything.

Speed's how far over how long. Velocity's speed with a direction stuck on it, five hundred knots northbound. If it's got a direction it's a vector: velocity, acceleration, force, and the wind in every triangle I ever drew. If it hasn't, it's a scalar. Speed, mass, time, temperature, energy. Acceleration is how fast your velocity changes. Our tankers went from parked to about 160 knots in forty seconds on a cold morning, call it four knots a second, and I felt every one of them in my kidneys. Slowing down counts too, just backward. So does a turn at a steady speed, since the direction keeps changing on you.

Anything going around a curve needs a pull toward the middle of it. That's centripetal force, center seeking. Swing a bucket on a rope and the rope's doing the pulling. Let go, and the bucket doesn't fly straight out from the middle. It goes off along the edge of the circle, the way it was headed that second. Faster, or a tighter turn, takes more pull. In a bank the wings tip and lend the airplane some of their lift for it, and your seat pushes you around the turn with it. That's the heavy feeling.

Drop a thing, keep the air off it, and it picks up about 9.8 meters a second of speed, every second. Call it ten if you're in a hurry, and on this test you are. That's g. Speed after a fall, g times the time. Distance, half of g times the time squared. Heavy and light come down together with no air in the way, which nobody believes till they see it. An Apollo crew dropped a hammer and a feather on the moon, on television. Same time. I watched it on my folks' set in the living room, and my dad slapped the side of it twice to keep the picture.

Try one with 10. Four seconds down, it's doing 40. Meters a second. Distance, half of 10 is 5, 4 squared's 16, call it 80 meters. The miss: somebody takes g times t, the speed, and writes that for the distance. I did it on a quiz in 1972. Speed climbs by the same amount each second. Distance piles up quicker, since each second starts out faster than the last. Square and a half for the distance. Neither for the speed.
How the exam asks it. A direction in the answer means a vector. No direction, a scalar.
Every launch I ever sat through was all three of Newton's laws at once. Somebody should've been selling tickets.

First law. Inertia. A thing sitting still stays still, and a thing moving keeps going, same speed, straight line, till some force makes it quit. That's your coffee in your lap when the tug stops short. The cup kept going. You didn't. The miss is thinking a moving thing needs pushing to keep moving. It doesn't. It needs a push to change. Out on the ramp friction's doing the stopping, all day long, and that's why it looks the other way.

Second law, the arithmetic one. Force is mass times acceleration, F equals m a. Same shove, twice the mass, half the acceleration. Weight's just the second law with gravity in it: mass times g. A 90 kilogram pilot in full gear weighs about 880 newtons here. On the moon g's about a sixth as much, so up there he'd weigh about 147, and his mass would still be 90 kilograms. Mass goes where you go. Weight depends on where you're standing. I'd have taken the moon's number at my flight physical. Try one. Net force of 1,800 newtons on a 600 kilogram trailer. Divide. Three meters a second, every second.

Third law. Forces come in pairs. Push on a thing and it pushes back just as hard, the other way. Four engines throw air and exhaust out the back, and the air throws the jet forward. Kick off the wall at the Y and you push the wall back, and the wall shoves you out into the lane. I swam there winter Tuesdays for years and felt that one every length. The miss is thinking the pair cancels out. It can't, because the two land on two different things, and each one moves its own. So on the test: something that keeps on doing what it was doing, first law. A number for force or mass, second. Two things shoving on each other, third.
How the exam asks it. Two things pushing on each other is the third law. One thing that won't change what it's doing is the first.

Momentum's mass times velocity. P equals m v. It's how hard a thing is to stop. A loaded tanker at taxi speed has more of it than a pickup on the interstate, and I never saw a tug driver argue with one. When the pieces only push on each other, a crash or a push apart, total momentum after is what it was before. Conservation of momentum.

Try one. A 4 kilogram cart rolls 3 meters a second into a 2 kilogram cart sitting still, and they latch. Before, 4 times 3. Twelve. After, still twelve, spread over 6 kilograms. Two meters a second. The miss is averaging the speeds, 3 and 0, and saying a meter and a half. Momentum counts the mass. Speeds don't average, and I'd write that on the back of my hand if I were you.

Friction pushes back on sliding. It depends on the two surfaces, and how hard they're pressed together, and how much area's touching hardly matters, which surprises everybody, me included. Getting a crate started usually takes more than keeping it going, since the friction on a thing sitting still runs higher than on one that's sliding. Any mover will tell you that, and charge you for it. I watched six of us get a dead tug rolling once on a January ramp, and two could keep it going after. Friction makes heat out of motion. Feel a brake after a long taxi and you'll believe it.

Gravity pulls every mass toward every other mass. Double the distance between two things and the pull drops to a quarter. Triple it, a ninth. That's the inverse square. The miss is halving it when the distance doubles, and I've seen colonels do it. Newton worked all that out without ever setting foot in an airplane, which has always bothered me a little. That same pull is what drags the oceans into tides, and I'll get to those.
How the exam asks it. Doubling the distance quarters gravity's pull. Don't halve it.
Pressure kept me alive at thirty thousand feet. The cabin held it in and the altimeter read it, and I never saw a lick of it.

Pressure's force spread over area. Pressure equals force divided by area. Same force, smaller area, more pressure, which is why a sharp knife cuts and a snowshoe doesn't sink. In a liquid it grows with depth, and with how dense the liquid is. It doesn't care one bit how wide the tank is. Fresh water adds about one pound per square inch every 2.31 feet down, about one atmosphere every ten meters. Air works the same way, only we live at the bottom of it. At sea level, about 14.7 pounds on every square inch, thinning as you climb. An altimeter's just a barometer with feet painted on its face, and I trusted mine more than some pilots.

Pascal's principle. Squeeze a fluid that's shut up in a line, and every inch of that line feels the squeeze, the same. Small piston on one end, big one on the other, and you've built a force multiplier. Force out over force in is big area over small area. Car jack, barber's chair, the brakes on your truck, and the chair at my dentist's that I'd rather not think about. The bill comes due in distance. The big piston moves less, same ratio, so what comes out in work never beats what went in. It only works because a liquid hardly squeezes. Get air in a brake line and the pedal goes soft. My first car was a '61 Falcon with a leak in the line, and I learned Pascal pumping that pedal down a hill outside Sedalia.

Try one. Say a shop press has a small piston of 2 square inches and a big one of 40. Lean on the small one with 50 pounds. That's 25 pounds per square inch all through the fluid, so the big one pushes 25 times 40. A thousand pounds. Push the small one down 10 inches and the big one comes up half an inch. Twenty times the force, a twentieth the travel, and no free lunch.

Floating's Archimedes. Whatever's in the water gets pushed up by the weight of the water it shoved aside. That's the whole rule. Shove aside its own weight before it's all the way under, and it floats. It comes down to density. Less dense than the fluid, it floats. More, it sinks. The share riding under the surface is its density over the fluid's. Ice is about nine tenths as dense as water, so nine tenths of an iceberg's under. Ask the Titanic. The miss is heavy things sink. A steel ship floats. It's the whole shape that counts, air inside and all.
How the exam asks it. Pressure's per square inch. When they offer you a wider tank, ask how deep, not how big.

A gas has no shape and no set volume. It fills whatever you put it in, and you can squeeze it, which you can't do to a liquid worth a darn. Three gas laws, one idea. Boyle's law: squeeze a gas, hold the temperature, and the pressure climbs in step. Half the volume, twice the pressure. Charles's law: warm a gas, hold the pressure, and it grows in step with its temperature in kelvins. A hot air balloon is Charles's law with a basket under it. I rode in one at the state fair in 1988, and the man flying it never said kelvin once. Warm one that's sealed in something rigid and the pressure goes up the same way. That's why a tire reads high after a long run, and why we checked ours cold, at four in the morning, with a flashlight in our teeth.

The trap's the temperature. These laws run on kelvins, never Celsius. To get kelvins, add 273 to the Celsius. Take a balloon from 20 Celsius to 40. That isn't double. In kelvins it's 293 to 313, about seven percent more, and that's all the balloon grows. Plenty of people double the Celsius, and they double the balloon right along with it.
How the exam asks it. A gas law with a temperature in it? Kelvins first, before anything else.

Work is a force times how far it moves something, in the direction it pushed. Joules again. Push a cart 8 meters with 15 newtons. That's 120 joules. Hold a box over your head an hour and you'll be wore out and you'll have done no work on it at all, since it didn't go anywhere. Walk it across the room at the same height, and by the book the force holding it up did nothing either. That force pointed up. The box went sideways. I argued with a nav school instructor about that once, and lost.

Energy does the work. Kinetic energy's energy of motion: half the mass, times the speed squared. Double the speed and you've got four times the energy, which is why a car at 60 takes about four times the braking distance it takes at 30. Potential energy's energy of position. Mass times g times height. Lift a 20 kilogram toolbox 2 meters and you've stored about 392 joules in it. Call it 400. Let go of it and that height turns back into speed on the way down, and then into a dent in the floor.

Energy doesn't get made and it doesn't get lost. It changes clothes, that's all. Conservation of energy. A roller coaster trades height for speed and back again, and friction skims a little off as heat every hill, which is why the second hill's lower. Power's how fast the work gets done. Work over time, in watts. Lift that toolbox in 2 seconds, about 200 watts. Take 4, and it's 100. Same work, half the power. The miss is mixing work with power, how much with how fast. A horsepower's about 746 watts, if they ask.
How the exam asks it. Twice the speed, four times the energy. The speed's squared in there.
Every crew chief I ever knew was a physicist nobody'd told. A longer handle on a stuck bolt is a lever.

A machine never gives you work for free. It trades. Less force over more distance, or the other way around. How much it multiplies your force is the mechanical advantage, load over effort. The six simple machines: lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw.

A lever turns on a fulcrum. Effort times its distance from the fulcrum equals load times its distance. Put 300 newtons half a meter from the fulcrum, push a meter and a half out the other side, and you need 100 newtons. A hundred times one and a half balances three hundred times a half. Your hand goes three times as far as the load. Three classes, named for what's in the middle. Fulcrum in the middle, first class: seesaw, pry bar, pliers. Load in the middle, second class: wheelbarrow, nutcracker. Effort in the middle, third class: tweezers, a broom, your own forearm. Third class costs you force and buys you speed.

Pulleys. One fixed pulley only turns your pull around, advantage of one, and you lift by hauling down. A movable pulley rides up with the load, so two strands hold it. Advantage of two. With a block and tackle, count the strands of rope holding up the moving block. Four strands, advantage four. A hundred newtons of pull raises 400, and you haul in four meters of rope for every meter it rises. Miss: counting pulleys instead of strands. Or counting the strand in your hand when it comes down off a fixed pulley overhead. That one's holding up nothing but your arm.

A ramp's an inclined plane, and its advantage is length over height. A 6 meter ramp up to a dock 1.5 meters high, advantage of 4. A 1,200 newton barrel takes about 300 to push up, friction aside, over four times the distance. A wedge is two ramps back to back. Axe head. A screw's a ramp wound around a post. A wheel and axle, a steering wheel or a screwdriver handle, multiplies by the wheel's radius over the axle's.

Gears make the same trade. A small gear driving a big one turns it slower and harder. Ten teeth driving forty turns the big one once for every four turns of the little one, with about four times the turning force. Swap them and you buy speed with force. Every one of these is the same deal as the hydraulics. Force times distance in, force times distance out, less a little for friction. Nobody's ever beaten it, and a fellow at the county fair in 1964 sold my dad a gadget that said it could.
How the exam asks it. Count rope strands holding the load, not pulleys. On any machine, more force means less distance.

Temperature's how hard the particles in a thing are jiggling, on average. Heat's energy on its way from something hotter to something colder. A tub of warm bathwater holds more heat than a cup of boiling water, though the cup's hotter. Three scales. Celsius puts water freezing at 0 and boiling at 100. Fahrenheit, 32 and 212. Kelvin starts at absolute zero, where the jiggling's as low as it goes. That's 0 kelvins, about minus 273 Celsius, and nothing gets colder. Its degrees are the same size as Celsius. Kelvin is Celsius plus 273. For Fahrenheit, Celsius times nine fifths, plus 32. Twenty Celsius: 36, plus 32, 68. I did that in my head for thirty years of weather briefings and got it wrong maybe twice that anybody caught. Minus 40 is the one spot where the two agree, and I've stood a ramp at it with my eyelashes frozen.

Heat gets around three ways. Conduction's contact, molecule to molecule, like a wrench left out on the ramp in July. Grab it. You'll learn. Convection's a fluid carrying it, warm air or water rising and cool sinking and around again, the way one radiator heats a whole room. Radiation needs nothing in between. It's light and infrared crossing empty space, and it's how the sun's heat gets here. The miss is calling a campfire's warmth on your face convection. The hot air's headed straight up. What's on your face is radiation.

Things grow when they warm and shrink when they cool. Most things, anyhow. Thermal expansion. It's the gaps in a bridge deck that go thump under your tires, and it's why a gallon of cold fuel weighs more than a gallon of warm. Water's the oddball. Densest at about 4 Celsius, and it gets bigger when it freezes, so ice floats. A lake freezes top down. That's the only reason a single fish in Missouri lives to see March.

Specific heat. How much heat it takes to warm a thing up. Water's runs high. Takes a pile of heat to warm it, gives a pile back cooling off, so a town on a big lake runs cooler all summer and warmer into the fall than a town fifty miles back from the shore. We flew out of a desert base one summer where the ramp hit a hundred and ten by three in the afternoon and you wanted a jacket at four in the morning. And when a thing changes state, every bit of the heat goes into the change. The temperature just sits. A pot of ice water, stirred, stays at zero till the last cube's gone. People expect the thermometer to climb. It waits.
How the exam asks it. Kelvin is Celsius plus 273. Heat that crosses empty space can only be radiation.

Matter comes in states. Solid keeps its shape and its volume. Liquid keeps its volume and takes the shape of whatever it's in. Gas takes both from the container. Heat a gas enough and it splits into charged pieces, a plasma. Lightning. The sun. And the blue fire I once watched crawl over our windscreen for twenty minutes above Kansas. St. Elmo's fire. The copilot said a word I won't repeat. It didn't hurt a thing.

The changes have names, and the test likes names. Solid to liquid, melting. Liquid to solid, freezing. Liquid to gas is vaporization, evaporating off the top or boiling all the way through. Gas to liquid's condensation, the sweat on a cold glass. Solid straight to gas, sublimation, like a mothball shrinking away in a closet, or snow going thin on a cold dry day without ever getting wet. Gas straight to solid, deposition, frost on a windshield. Boiling depends on the pressure on top. Lower it and water boils cooler. Raise it and water boils hotter, which is the whole trick inside a pressure cooker.

Density's mass over volume. Water's 1 gram a cubic centimeter. A kilogram a liter. About 8.34 pounds a gallon. A 600 gram block that takes up 1,000 cubic centimeters comes out 0.6, so it floats, six tenths under. Surface tension is water hanging onto itself at the top. It lets a needle lie on the surface and a water strider walk, and it's why a drop stands up round instead of going flat. Water holding on to water is cohesion. Water holding on to something else, glass or cloth or a paper towel, is adhesion. When the stick to the wall beats the stick to itself, water climbs a skinny tube on its own, and that's capillary action. It's how a paper towel drinks a spill and how a tree gets water up out of the ground. In a narrow glass tube water's surface curves up at the edges. Mercury's curves down, since mercury would rather hold on to itself.

A physical change leaves the stuff what it was. Melting, bending, sugar in your coffee. A chemical change makes something new. Burning, rusting, baking. Signs it's chemical: a gas you didn't have before, a color change, heat or light given off, a solid falling out of a clear liquid. Mass isn't made or lost either way. Burn a log and the ash weighs less, sure, but count the smoke and the gases and it all adds back up.
How the exam asks it. Solid straight to gas is sublimation. Gas straight to solid is deposition. They'll offer you both.

Chemistry was my worst grade in college, a C, and the man was being generous. So here it is the way I finally got it. An atom's a small heavy nucleus with electrons around it. In the nucleus you've got protons, a plus charge each, and neutrons, no charge at all. Around it, electrons, a minus charge each, light as nothing. If the nucleus were a marble on the fifty yard line, the electrons would be gnats up in the cheap seats. The count of protons is the atomic number, and it decides the element. Six is carbon. Always. Pencil lead, coal, a diamond, every one of them six. Eight is oxygen. Protons plus neutrons is the mass number. Same element, different count of neutrons, is an isotope. Gain or lose electrons and you've got an ion, a charged atom. Lose one, it's plus. Gain one, minus.

Try one. Eleven protons, 12 neutrons. Atomic number 11. That's sodium. Mass number 23. Lose an electron and it's a sodium ion, plus one. The miss: changing the protons and calling it an ion. Change the protons and it isn't the same element anymore. It's somebody else.

The periodic table runs by atomic number, left to right, top to bottom. A row's a period. A column's a group. Everything in a group has the same count of electrons in its outer shell, and that's why they behave like brothers. The far left column, under hydrogen, is the alkali metals. Drop a chunk of sodium in water and stand back. My high school chemistry teacher did it off the river bridge in 1968, and they talked about it in town for a month. One column in from the right edge are the halogens, chlorine and fluorine, each one hungry for one more electron. The right edge itself is the noble gases, full up and quiet, like the heritage room on a Saturday. Metals sit on the left and through the middle, and they conduct. Nonmetals sit off to the right.

Atoms hang on to each other with bonds, and there's two kinds worth knowing. Ionic: one atom hands electrons to another, usually a metal to a nonmetal, and the two charged ions cling. Table salt. Covalent: two nonmetals share electrons. Water, carbon dioxide, the fuel in a tanker. An element's one kind of atom. A compound's two or more kinds bonded in a fixed recipe, water always two hydrogens to one oxygen. A mixture is things together but not bonded, any amounts, and you can pull them apart without chemistry. Salt water. Air. Gravel. Boil off the water and the salt's still in the pan, which I know because I've burned a pan that way.
How the exam asks it. Protons pick the element. Neutrons pick the isotope. Electrons pick the charge.

The pH scale runs 0 to 14. Seven's neutral, pure water. Under 7 is acid, lemon juice and vinegar and what's in a battery. Over 7 is base: baking soda, ammonia, the bleach a water plant feeds. Each whole step is ten times. A pH of 2 is ten times more acidic than 3, a hundred times more than 4, and a thousand times more than 5. Mix an acid with a base and they drag each other toward the middle, and you get a salt and water. Neutralization. It's why you'd put baking soda on spilled battery acid.

Radioactive atoms break down on their own, steady as a dripping faucet. Half life's just the time it takes for half of a sample to go. Then half of whatever's left goes in the next stretch, and so on down. Start with 96 grams, and say the half life's 2 hours. After two hours you've got 48. Four hours, 24. Six, 12. At eight hours there's 6 left, and it never does get all the way to nothing. The miss is thinking it's all gone after two half lives. Half of a half isn't zero. It's a quarter, and a quarter's still sitting there.

What comes flying off a breaking atom is radiation, and they'll want three names. Alpha's a slow, heavy lump, two protons and two neutrons, and a sheet of paper stops it cold. Beta's a fast electron. A thin sheet of aluminum'll do for that one. Gamma's a ray, light's big cousin, and you want thick lead or a wall of concrete between you and it. My dad's wristwatch had a radium dial that glowed green, and he wore it to bed for thirty years. Getting energy out of a nucleus on purpose, there's two ways. Fission splits a heavy one, uranium, into two smaller pieces. That's the power plant down by Fulton. Fusion jams light ones, hydrogen, together into something heavier, and that's the sun. Split heavy, fuse light.
How the exam asks it. One pH step is ten times. Count the steps and multiply the tens. Never add them.
I never touched a wire on that airplane. I knew which breakers to pull, and I knew why.

Charge comes in plus and minus. Like charges push apart. Unlike pull together. Rub a comb on a wool sweater and electrons hop from one to the other, and now the comb's charged. Static. The protons stay home in the nucleus, so it's always the electrons doing the traveling. Conductors let charge flow. Metals, copper for most wiring, and salty water. Insulators don't. Rubber, glass, plastic, dry wood.

Current's the flow of charge, in amperes. Voltage is the push behind it, in volts. Resistance is how hard the path pushes back, in ohms. The avionics shop had it painted on the wall in letters a foot high, and I never saw anybody look at it. Ohm's law ties the three together. Volts equal amps times ohms, so amps are volts over ohms, and if that won't stay put, draw the triangle the way the boys in avionics did. Put a 6 volt lantern battery across a 3 ohm bulb and you get 2 amps, enough to find your keys by. Power's volts times amps. Watts. The toaster in our kitchen pulls 10 amps off 120 volts. That's 1,200 watts, and it still burns one side of the bread.

There's two ways to hook things up. Series is one road, and everything's strung out on it like ducks crossing the river road. The same current runs through all of it, the ohms add, and if one bulb quits the road's cut and they all go dark. Runway edge lights run on a loop like that, with a little transformer at every fixture so one dead lamp won't black out the whole side, and somebody learned that the hard way before my time. Parallel's separate roads, side by side, and every one of them gets the whole voltage. Add up the branches and you've got what the battery's putting out. Now here's the part that sounds wrong. The total resistance comes out lower than any one branch. You opened another road, same as they did on the beltway in '79, and traffic moved better, not worse. Two equal resistors side by side, you get half of one. My mother's Christmas lights were series, and every December my dad stood on a kitchen chair on Christmas Eve, cussing, testing bulbs one at a time. Your house is parallel, which is why the fridge keeps running when the bulb in the hall goes. Fuses and breakers go in series, out front of whatever they protect, so when one pops, everything behind it quits.

Try one. Two 10 ohm resistors on 20 volts. Hook them in series and it's 20 ohms, so 1 amp. Side by side it's 5 ohms and 4 amps, two down each branch. Folks add resistances that sit side by side all the time, and I did it on a trainer board myself in 1974. Count the roads before you add a thing.

Batteries push current one way, like a one way street downtown, and that's direct current, DC. Your wall outlet flips it back and forth sixty times a second. Alternating current, AC, and that's the hum you hear off the gray can on a pole on a hot night. That can's a transformer. Two coils of wire wound on one iron core, and the trick is the turns. More turns on the side going out than coming in, it steps the volts up. Fewer, it steps them down. The power company runs it across the county at thousands of volts because it wastes less that way, and the can by your house knocks it down to 120 for the toaster. Only works on AC, though. I watched an airman hook one to a battery on a trainer board once, and the sergeant let him go at it for an hour.

Current makes magnetism too. Wind wire into a coil, run current through it, there's your electromagnet. More turns, more current, iron in the middle, and it's stronger. Kill the current and it lets go, and that's how the crane at the junkyard on Route 9 drops a car. Run the idea backward and you've got a generator. Shove a magnet through a coil and current flows. Magnets have a north end and a south. Like ends shove apart. Unlike ends grab. The earth's one big magnet. A compass needle's a little one, lining itself up. Ours rode up on the glare shield in a little bowl of fluid. Swung like a drunk in every bank. Whiskey compass, the pilots called it. It never quit on me. I can't say that for the Doppler.
How the exam asks it. Side by side is parallel. Full push on every branch, and the ohms go down.

A wave carries energy along without hauling the water off with it. Sit on a dock at Lake of the Ozarks and watch a swell go under your bobber. The bobber goes up, goes down, and stays right where it was. Crest to crest is the wavelength. How many go by in a second is the frequency, in hertz. How tall they are is the amplitude. Speed is frequency times wavelength. A sound at 340 meters a second and 680 hertz is half a meter long. Same speed, higher frequency, shorter waves. A piccolo throws short ones. A tuba throws long ones.

Sound's a push wave. Squeeze, stretch, squeeze, all through whatever it's in, so it has to be in something. No air, no sound. Out in space a shout goes nowhere at all. About 340 meters a second in air, faster in water, faster again in steel. Pitch is frequency. Loud is amplitude. An echo's sound bouncing back. Coming at you, the noise bunches its waves up and the pitch climbs. Going away, it drops. Every freight train through Tolliver does it. That's the Doppler effect, and it's how the Doppler radar on my airplane read our ground speed. Until the day it didn't, and then I did it with a pencil.

Light's an electromagnetic wave, and it needs nothing at all to travel through. About 300,000 kilometers a second. 186,000 miles. The electromagnetic waves make one long family, longest wave and lowest frequency first: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X rays, gamma rays. Visible runs red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Red's the longest wave, violet the shortest. The miss is setting ultraviolet below visible because you can't see it. It's above. More frequency, more energy, and that's why it burns you on a ramp in June.

Light bounces. Light bends. Off a mirror, it leaves at the same angle it hit, measured off a line straight out of the glass. Reflection. Into glass or water, it changes speed and bends. Refraction. Stand a fence post in a creek and it looks snapped off right at the waterline. A prism bends each color its own amount and fans white light into a rainbow, and Patrice has one hanging in the kitchen window that throws them on the ceiling every afternoon about four. Fat in the middle, convex, a lens pulls light together to a point. That's your magnifying glass. I set a pile of leaves smoking with one in 1959, and my mother had words with me. Thin in the middle, concave, it spreads light out. Every star I shot low through that sextant port sat a hair higher than it really was, because the air bent it on the way in. There was a table for that. There was a table for everything.
How the exam asks it. Sound needs air or water or steel to ride on. Light doesn't need a thing. Up the family means more frequency, more energy, shorter waves.
Navigators were about the last fellows paid to look up. Learn the sky like you learned that ramp.

Air's layered. Bottom one's the troposphere, from the ground up to about 8 kilometers over the poles and 18 over the equator, and near all the weather's in it, which is why I spent my working life staring at it. It cools as you climb, about 2 degrees Celsius every thousand feet, so the top of a thunderhead runs colder than your freezer. Next up, the stratosphere, with the ozone in it. Long range jets like to cruise near its floor, where the ride smooths out. Above that the mesosphere, where meteors burn up. Then the thermosphere, with the northern lights in it, then the exosphere, thinning out to nothing at all. The air's about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 oxygen. I kept that on a card in my flight suit, and I couldn't tell you why.

Air moves from high pressure toward low. A high's sinking air, and sinking air dries out, so a high's mostly clear. A low is rising air, and rising air cools and clouds up and rains. So a falling barometer means a low's on its way. A front's where two air masses meet. Cold front shoves under the warm air fast and steep: a narrow line of thunderstorms, gusts, then cooler clearer air behind. I rode through one over Nebraska in 1984 and wore a whole thermos of coffee home on my flight suit. Warm front slides up over the cold slow: a long gray spell of low clouds and steady rain. Relative humidity is the water the air's holding over the most it could hold at that temperature. Cool the air and the same water's a bigger share, so the humidity climbs. At 100 percent you've hit the dew point, and the water condenses. That's a cloud. On the ground, fog. I sat out more fog in Kansas City than I care to count. Dispatch ran on fronts. I'd hold a freighter forty minutes for a cold front, take an earful from a man in a tie, and then watch the line come through right on time and blow his coffee off the ramp.

The wind doesn't run straight from high to low, either. The earth turns under it, and that bends moving air to the right up here and to the left south of the equator. That's the Coriolis effect, and it's why our lows wind up counterclockwise. Up near the top of the troposphere there's a river of fast wind called the jet stream, mostly running west to east, a hundred knots and better in winter. Eastbound we rode it. Westbound we fought it, and you could read which in the fuel log.

Earth spins on its axis once a day, and that's your day and night. Goes around the sun once a year. Spin's rotation, the trip around's revolution, and I've watched grown men swap those two at a briefing. The axis leans about 23 and a half degrees, and the lean's what makes seasons. The half tipped toward the sun gets it higher overhead and the long days. Distance hasn't got a thing to do with it. We're closest to the sun in early January, and you've stood on a Missouri ramp in January. Patrice still says summer's when we're closer, and I let her.

Moon's around us about once a month. One night in the den I showed Patrice's nephew with the shade off a lamp and an orange on a pencil. Hold it out, turn slow. Half that orange stays lit, always. What you get from where you stand is some of the lit half, a sliver, a half, all of it, back down. Phases. It's not our shadow. Our shadow on the moon's an eclipse, and that makes the paper, lunar at a full moon. A solar eclipse is the moon parked in front of the sun, new moon. The boy ate the orange. Tides come off the moon's pull, mostly. It raises two bulges in the ocean, one on the side facing it and one on the far side, so most coasts get two high tides a day, and they're biggest when sun and moon line up, at new and full. A navigator who'd crossed the Pacific told me he could tell the date by the beach at Guam. I believed him for years.

The sun's a star. Middling, as stars go. Out from it, Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, then Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos, if you want the order on your scratch paper. First four are rock. Last four are big balls of gas and ice, and Jupiter's the biggest thing out there but the sun. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to get here. If it quit on us, we'd have eight minutes before anybody knew.

Under your boots there's a thin rind of rock, the crust. Under that the mantle, solid rock that creeps a few centimeters a year. Then the outer core, liquid iron and nickel, the only layer that pours. Then a solid inner core, solid only because it's squeezed so hard. The crust's cracked into plates that drift about as fast as your fingernails grow, and the earthquakes and volcanoes bunch up along the cracks. Rock comes three ways. Igneous cooled from melted rock. Obsidian is lava that cooled so fast it went to black glass, and pumice is lava so full of gas it'll float in a bucket. Sedimentary is layers pressed flat, sandstone, limestone, and that's where you find the fossils. Metamorphic got cooked by heat and pressure without melting. Marble from limestone. Slate from shale. There's a slate chalkboard in the heritage room older than I am.
How the exam asks it. Rotation is a day and revolution is a year. Phases are the angle, and eclipses are the shadow.
Decision one. Twelve seconds a word.
Behind him on the fridge, Saturday's square said PRACTICE TEST, 5 HRS, ME ON THE CLOCK, in green, and under that, small, in his black, 2019.
The analogies went the way they went at Vern's. At eight minutes the timer beeped. Time.

He took the packet, slid the next one over, and set the timer for twenty nine. Arithmetic: pump rates, fuel, a train out of Kansas City, and she was quicker at those than she'd ever been. Then WORD KNOWLEDGE, twenty five in five minutes. Twelve seconds a word.
Number fourteen was DISSEMBLE. She knew the word. She'd known it since high school, and she'd never liked it.
DISSEMBLE: closest in meaning. Which one does Kit mark?
C. Put on a false front.

She marked it and went on. To dissemble was to keep a face in front of the truth, and you could do it without saying one false word. She'd stayed for the inspection. Boyd had asked her to. All of it true, and all of it standing in front of a nineteen. She was on fifteen before Graham's timer had moved much.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Dissemble. To hide what's real behind a face, put on a front. Closest in meaning is whichever one fits every place the word goes. It's from the old Latin for disguising yourself, same root as similar. Looking like what you aren't. Then don't trust it to look like its cousins, because one of them is a trap with a wrench in it. Know it, or take your best root guess and get on to the next.
Decision two. The circle in the square.
Then MATH KNOWLEDGE, twenty five in twenty two minutes. Graham set the timer and sat back with his coffee. Out the window the neighbor's dog was digging at something by the fence again.

She'd run Vern's four sets on his egg timer, twenty two minutes each, and gone over her misses afterward with no clock at all. She knew where her time went now. At eleven minutes she was on number twelve, about where she wanted to be.
Number fourteen. Circle in a square, and they wanted the corners. She looked at it, and it didn't open.
A circle she can't see into, and the clock running. What should Kit do with number fourteen?
A. Put her best guess down, circle the number, and go on.
B. Leave it blank, and come back to it if there's time.
C. Flip to the back page, and work the rest from the end.
D. Stay on it till she can see how the circle fits.
She put B. It looked about right for corners that size. She circled fourteen on her scratch sheet and went on. Fifteen was a straight line through two points, and she had it in thirty seconds.

Right. Log it. That's pace, Sergeant. A guess on the slow one, a mark so you can find it, and on to the next. A guess costs you nothing. A blank never helped anybody. If there's time left over at the end, go back to your circles. The corners are the square less the circle: side squared, minus pi times the radius squared, and the radius is half the side. A side of 10 is 100 less about 78.5, so a little over 21 for all four corners. On Math Knowledge you get about fifty three seconds a problem, and no single problem's worth two of them.
When the timer went she was back on fourteen. The circle had finally opened, and she changed her B to a D with about two seconds left. She didn't know yet whether that was smart.

Reading went by in twenty four minutes. Situational Judgment took thirty five, a stack of young lieutenants with problems that weren't hers, and she found she knew what Vern would say about most of them. Then Graham set the timer for fifteen and pointed at the fridge, which meant food. She ate a sandwich standing up and didn't look at her coat.

Where the inventory went, Graham had left forty five minutes on the clock and nothing to answer, because on the day she'd be that tired. She sat through them with her eyes shut and heard every car go by on Orchard Street.
Then PHYSICAL SCIENCE, twenty in ten minutes. Thirty seconds each. Graham taught this five days a week, and in nine years she'd never once asked him to teach her any of it.

Number six showed two open tanks of water filled to the same depth. One was tall and narrow. The other was as wide as a barn. Graham had drawn them himself, with a little cartoon cow by the wide one. For scale, she guessed.
Same depth of water, one tank narrow and one wide. Where's the pressure at the bottom higher?
A. The narrow one. There's less floor to spread it on.
B. Neither. The depth sets it, not the width.
C. The same, since water weighs the same per gallon.
D. The wide one. There's more water in it.

Neither. It came so fast it surprised her. Out at the dead end of Cooper Road, the pressure was whatever the tower on the hill made it. Not how much water. How high. Two point three one feet to the pound, and she'd done that one at three in the morning more times than she'd ever tell anybody. Marked. Most of her thirty seconds still left for seven.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Depth. And how dense the liquid is. That's all pressure in a liquid cares about. Never width. Wide tank, more water, sure. It's spread over more floor. Each square inch gets the same as the skinny one's. About a pound per square inch every 2.31 feet of fresh water, and you knew that one before I did. The miss is more water, more pressure. I heard a city councilman in Kansas City stand up and argue for a fatter water tower once, to get his ward more pressure. Nobody had the heart.
Decision four. Minus four, plus seven.

Then TABLE READING. One grid the size of the whole page. Columns ran minus ten to ten across the top, rows ran ten down to minus ten along the side, plus numbers on top. Forty questions in seven minutes. Graham had run the grid off on the copier in the teachers' lounge, and it had a gray stripe down the middle where the glass was dirty. She put her left hand flat on the table and her pencil in her right.
Number twenty two asked for X minus 4, Y plus 7. She went across the top to minus 4, ran down, and got 63. The choices were 61, 64, 66, 67 and 58. Sixty three wasn't any of them.
Her number isn't one of the five choices. What should Kit do about it?
A. Take 64, the one closest to what she found.
B. Run the same path again, only slower.
C. Go back to the edge labels and find it again.
D. Leave it, and save the ten seconds for the next one.

She took her pencil back to the edges. X across the top, minus 4. Y down the side, plus 7, up near the top, where Graham had put the plus numbers. She'd run down from the zero row and landed on minus 7. The cell at minus 4, plus 7 said 66, right there in the choices, two over from the 64 she'd almost taken.

That'll hold, Sergeant. When your number isn't there, you slipped. You didn't find a misprint. Go back to the labels, not to the cell you were staring at. X runs across the top, Y down the side, and check which way the side runs, plus at the top or at the bottom. The usual slips are a swapped X and Y, and a lost minus sign. Accuracy first. On this subtest you get about ten seconds a question, and that's enough to find a cell twice.
Decision five. The paper on the table.

Instrument Comprehension came and went in five minutes, the dials she'd frozen on in 2019, and she didn't freeze. She didn't do well, either, and she knew it as she went. Block Counting, then Aviation Information, and a little before noon Graham said it for the last time.

He squared the eleven packets into a pile, took the binder clips off and put them in his shirt pocket, and slid the stack into his school bag. Then he kissed the top of her head and went out to mow the side yard, which didn't need it.
She slept two hours on the couch. At six she made eggs, because eggs were what they had, and when the plates were in the sink she went to the hook by the door and took the sheet out of her coat.

She unfolded it on the kitchen table, under the light, where she'd taken the test that morning. Pilot 19. Under it, in Vern's capitals, ACUITY. Graham sat down across from her, in the same chair he'd timed her from, and waited.
The sheet's on the table between them. What does Kit say to him?
A. Say it in her own words: the nineteen, the yes, and what she let him think.
B. Tell him she's sorry first, and ask him not to be angry.
C. Point at the numbers and let the paper say it.
D. Start with that winter: she was twenty five, the inspection was real, and Boyd really asked.

It wasn't Boyd. The scores came back that fall, and Pilot was nineteen, and it has to be twenty five. Then Boyd asked me to stay for the inspection, and I said yes. Yes meant I never had to say nineteen to you. I told you he'd asked, and I let that be the reason. She stopped there. She'd thought there would be more, something about being twenty five, and there wasn't.

Right. Log it. Integrity. The plain kind. The fact first, in your own words, nothing stacked in front of it. You didn't ask him for a thing. Not forgiveness, not patience. On the test, the action that owns the problem flat out and leaves the other fellow his own reaction is where the key leans. Second time you've told it in the right order. It doesn't get shorter.

For a long time Graham didn't say anything. He picked up the sheet and read it again, all the way to the bottom, same as he'd read a lab report. Then he put one finger on the word in the margin, the way he'd point at a wrong answer, only gentler. Whose writing is that? It isn't yours.
Vern's. It's his word, and it's his to tell. He nodded as if that was the one fair thing on the table, and he set the sheet down square with the edge.
In January, when you told me you wanted it, I took a minute before I said okay. You noticed. I was doing some math of my own. I'd made my peace with the slot before I opened my mouth.
I've had three weeks to guess what that 2019 was. I didn't guess this. It's not the slot. You let me think it was Boyd for seven years.
He looked at the dark window over the sink. I used to hold it against him a little. Every Christmas party. There's the guy.
He's said it, and he's waiting. What does Kit do now?
A. Ask him, gently, what he needs from her right now.
B. Remind him there's a crib in the garage he never told her about.
C. Go up to bed, and give him the kitchen to himself tonight.
D. Tell him "I did," and stay put at the table.

I did. She didn't add the part about the inspection being real. She didn't get up. He looked at the window. She let him. The clock over the stove was loud enough to count. After a while he said Boyd's name once more, not to her, and shook his head.

That's the fix I'd have taken. You owned it in two words, and then you stayed in the room for what it did to him. No defense, no fix, no leaving him alone with it. Integrity's the competency here, and the key leans hard toward owning a thing outright over explaining it. The staying is the part people skip.
Near ten he got up, turned on the side light, and stood at the back door with his hand on the knob. Come out to the garage a minute.
Friday she'd put the tarp back the way it had been, and left it for him to lift.

The motion light came on over them. He went past the mower to the back wall and took hold of the corner of the blue tarp, and before he could lift it, she said it. I saw it Friday, when I came out for the battery. I put the tarp back.
He lifted the corner anyway and folded it back over the top rail, and the crib stood there in the light with its paper tag still tied to the post.

Two springs ago I stood right there in that door and asked you if this was the year we tried for a baby. You said after the KC-46 talk. That Saturday there was an estate sale out on Mill Road. Forty dollars. I didn't even haggle.
After your degree. After the inspection. After the deployment. After the new jets. He stopped on the second one. The inspection was the lie too.
It wasn't a question, and she didn't make him ask it. Yes.
I'm not asking you for an answer tonight. I'm asking you not to hand me another after.
He's asked her for no more afters. What does Kit tell him?
A. Tell him yes, this year, and see how the rest falls out.
B. Tell him she doesn't know yet, and she won't say after.
C. Tell him after the board, in July, and mean it this time.
D. Tell him it's his call, and she'll go along with whatever he wants.

I don't know yet. I want to fly, Graham. I don't know how this fits next to that, and I'm not going to put a word on it to make tonight easier. He looked at the crib a while. Okay. No beat in front of it, and no after behind it. He put the tarp corner back where it had been, and on the way out he switched off the light by the door, though it would've gone off by itself.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Integrity and Communication together. He asked for no more afters and you didn't give him one, and you didn't give him a yes you couldn't stand behind either. You told him the true state of things, unfinished as it is. The test rewards the honest answer over the comfortable one, and so do the people you'll lead.
Sunday morning the 2019 was gone off the whiteboard. There was a gray smear in Saturday's square where a thumb had been, and the green around it was left alone.

Graham went to the hardware store at nine and came back at noon with a box of deck screws and nothing else. He was kind to her all morning, careful about it, the way people are kind in a hospital hallway.
Her mother had texted Saturday afternoon. Kit read it again after lunch, on the back step.
A text from Rhonda. How did the big practice test go Kitty?? Darlene says five hours is longer than her wedding. Call me
Rhonda still had the Boyd version. She'd had it for seven years, and she'd told it at her own table, proud of a daughter who stayed for her people. Boyd was next, at drill.
Her mother's text is still sitting there from yesterday. What does Kit do about her?
A. Call her, and ask for an hour at her table next Sunday.
B. Text back that it went fine, and leave the rest where it is.
C. Call her now, and tell her all of it over the phone.
D. Ask Graham to call her, so she won't have to say it twice.

She called. Rhonda picked up on the first ring, the way she always did, as if she'd had the phone in her hand the whole time. It went fine, Mom. Long. I'll have the numbers this week. Then, before she could talk herself out of it: Can I come by next Sunday, when drill lets out? About four. There's something from 2019 I should've told you. I want to say it at your table. The line went quiet. Is it bad? It's old. Then I'll make a roast, her mother said, and Kit laughed for the first time since Friday.

Right. Log it. Communication, with a time on it. She hears it from you, in person, and soon, and she knows it's coming, so it doesn't reach her from somebody else first. Boyd still hears it before she does, and that's the right order. He's the one who carried it.
Tuesday at Vern's she said it with her coat still on. Graham knows. Vern looked at her over the percolator. The index card still stood against it, where it had stood for four weeks.
That's one. He didn't ask how it went. At the end of the night he handed her the week's log, and she read it at the stop sign by the grain elevator with the dome light on.

My log, twenty two January, oh one. Minus eighteen Celsius on the ramp. Trucks metered twenty thousand gallons. Gauges said one hundred thirty eight thousand pounds. The same gallons in August made one thirty two. Did not argue with the gauges.

Graham had put it on the whiteboard back in February, before any of this, one of her blue blocks: WED, MY LAB, 3:30. She hadn't known if it still stood, and she'd decided she wouldn't ask. At three on Wednesday he texted her the room number, as if she might not know it.

Room 114 smelled like the gas taps and a hundred sophomores. He'd set up three stations down the long black bench and pulled a stool up to the first one for her. His school bag was on the floor by his desk, and she could see her eleven packets in it under a stack of lab reports. He hadn't scored them.

He saw her see the bag. Third period took a unit test Monday. Eleven of them came in under half. He was setting two cylinders out on the bench and didn't look up from them. Some of them cried. Then they came in at lunch and we went through it, one at a time. You could've brought me a nineteen. She nodded. Then she showed him Vern's log, because it was what she'd brought.
He read it and handed it back. Your navigator didn't argue with the gauges. Good for him. Same gallons, six thousand more pounds. Where did they come from?
A. The cold put weight into it, so cold fuel has more mass.
B. The fuel shrank in the cold, so each gallon held more fuel.
C. It's thicker cold, so a gallon of it weighs more.
D. The cold throws the gauges off, and she wouldn't trust them.

She said it the way she'd have said it on the ramp. Same stuff, packed tighter. Graham nodded once. He got a bottle of cooking oil out of the lab fridge and warmed half of it on the hot plate, and she watched him measure a hundred milliliters of each, slower than he needed to. On the balance the cold one came out about three grams heavier. She thought of the hose in January, so cold it bit through her gloves. Density. Nobody added any fuel. Same fuel, smaller space.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Density. Mass over volume. Cool almost anything and it pulls in a little, same mass in less room, so a gallon of it weighs more. That's why I planned fuel in pounds and never gallons, twenty one years at the nav table and thirty one at dispatch. Pounds are what the wings carry. Jet fuel runs about 6.6 pounds a gallon on an August afternoon, closer to 6.9 on a January morning, and the truck driver doesn't care which. I watched a new dispatcher forget it once and have a captain on the phone in about four minutes, and the captain was not a patient man. Where folks miss is thinking the cold added mass. Mass never changed. The room it took up did.

Station two was a pair of plastic syringes with a foot of clear tubing between them and blue water through the whole thing. The skinny one was what you'd use to get a pill into a cat. The fat one she could've stuck her thumb in. Masking tape on each in his printing, 1 SQ CM and 5 SQ CM, on straight, which with Graham meant he'd had time on his hands. He hadn't said her name once since three thirty.

Your truck's brakes. You push a little piston at the pedal, and there's a fat one out at every wheel, with brake fluid between. The jet's the same, except a pump does your pushing, and you'd know how loud. He put two fingers on the skinny one. Say I push this one in ten centimeters with twenty newtons. What's the fat one do?
A. Pushes with four newtons, and moves fifty centimeters.
B. Pushes with a hundred newtons, and moves the same ten centimeters.
C. Pushes with twenty newtons. Same pressure, same push.
D. Pushes with a hundred newtons, and moves two centimeters.

Twenty newtons on one square centimeter, and that same squeeze all through the blue water. The fat one had five square centimeters for it to push on, so a hundred newtons. A fifth as far. It climbed two centimeters, right on the mark, and the blue in the tube shivered. He worked it on a paper towel from the dispenser with a ballpoint, which tore it. A hundred times two. Twenty times ten. Same work, both ends of the tube. Water doesn't give you anything for free.

That'll hold, Sergeant. That's Pascal. Squeeze a shut in fluid anywhere and you've squeezed it everywhere, same amount. Pressure's force over area. Fat piston, five times the area, five times the shove. And it goes a fifth as far. That's the bill. It always comes. Folks grab the force and forget the bill. Two two eight's gear comes up on that rule every flight. Has since Kennedy. Works because water hardly squeezes. Put a bubble in the line and you're pushing on a sponge, and you know that better than I do.

Station three was the one he liked, she could tell. Plywood, a battery pack out of the supply closet, two bulbs in screw sockets, red and black clip leads all over. Somebody'd written 12 V on the pack in Sharpie, and somebody else had added a smiley face. Gum under the bench lip, gray and old. She'd have bet a week's pay he knew whose.

Call each bulb six ohms. Close enough for government work. Side by side, each one with its own road home. That's parallel. Last clip, and both bulbs lit up hard enough to make her squint. So. How much current's coming out of that battery?
A. Seventy two amps: twelve times six.
B. One amp: twelve volts over twelve ohms.
C. Four amps, two through each of the paths.
D. Two amps: twelve volts over six ohms.

Each road got the whole twelve volts, so two amps a road, and two roads. Graham unclipped one bulb. The other one didn't so much as flicker. She kept her eyes on the one still lit. That's your house, more or less. Every outlet gets the full hundred and twenty. The toaster doesn't care if the lamp's on.

Right. Log it. That's parallel, and he set it up so you'd see it. Each branch gets all twelve volts, so you work them one at a time with Ohm's law and add. Twelve over six is two, and two branches makes four. Taken together the two bulbs come out three ohms, lower than either one, since there's a second road now. I sat on the Kansas City beltway enough evenings to know what one more lane does at five o'clock. If you got twelve, you added six and six. That's series, one road through both, one amp, and a couple of dim orange bulbs.
Friday morning she came off nights at ten after seven. The house was empty. Graham had left for school.

The coffee was on, the pot about half full and starting to smell burnt, which meant he'd made it for her and not for himself. On the kitchen table, squared to the edge, were her eleven packets, every page marked in his red pen. Sometime after she'd left for the plant last night, he'd sat down at this table and done all of it.
On the top packet was a yellow sticky note in his printing.
A R, twenty one out of twenty five. Good.
Under it, on the cover page, he'd written every block's number in a column, the way he wrote grades in his book.

Verbal Analogies, twenty of twenty five. Arithmetic Reasoning, twenty one of twenty five. Word Knowledge, nineteen of twenty five. Math Knowledge, twenty of twenty five. Reading, twenty of twenty five. Situational Judgment, twenty five of thirty two. Physical Science, thirteen of twenty. Table Reading, thirty three of forty. Instrument Comprehension, fourteen of twenty five. Block Counting, twenty two of thirty. Aviation Information, eleven of twenty.
Eleven numbers in red pen on the cover page. How should Kit read them?
A. Look up a chart online that turns raw scores into percentiles.
B. Drill Physical Science first, since Graham can teach it.
C. Add it all up, and see how far she's come since 2019.
D. Block by block, against the four blocks Pilot leans on.

She got a pen and went down the cover page against the four that Pilot leans on. Math Knowledge, Table Reading, Instrument Comprehension, Aviation Information. Table Reading was fine. Math she already knew about. Instruments was fourteen of twenty five, and Aviation was eleven of twenty, on a jet she'd been crewing since she was twenty two. She opened the Aviation packet to see what she'd missed, and it was all from inside the airplane, every miss a thing a pilot would know and a crew chief wouldn't. She wrote IC and AI at the top of a clean page and boxed them twice.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Read a practice score where it counts. Pilot leans on Math Knowledge, Table Reading, Instrument Comprehension and Aviation Information, so those four tell you the most about the composite you need. Then open a low one and look for the pattern in the misses. Real percentiles come only from the real test, so don't try to turn raw numbers into one. Physical Science feeds no composite in the 2015 pamphlet. Work on it, but not first.
She read the sticky note again. AR 21/25. Good.

Graham wrote Good on a lab report when it was true. Not once when it wasn't. His sophomores had that figured out by October, and the smart ones by the second week. Every page of eleven packets, marked, at the same table she'd told him at. And the only word on any of it that wasn't a number was that one. Under the one block that earned it.
She read it a third time and still couldn't tell which part of the week it sat under.

She peeled the note off the packet and a little of the cover page came along. She thumbed it flat. Her coat was on the hook. In the inside pocket, same as always, the sheet, folded under Vern's two logs, ACUITY on the inside where nobody'd see it. She stuck Graham's yellow note on the outside of the fold. Next time that sheet came out of her pocket, his note would come out first.
She tore a sheet off his pad of yellow notes and wrote one of her own, in her printing, which was worse than his.
P S, thirteen out of twenty. Will you teach me the seven?

She stuck it on the coffee maker, over the switch. He'd be home at four and she'd be asleep, so he'd find it before he found her. She shut the pot off and poured what was left into the mug with the chipped handle. Six o'clock coffee at a quarter to eight. She drank it anyway, at the sink, boots still on.
